title: The Berman–Hartmanis isomorphism conjecture
formal: For every pair of languages A,B⊆{0,1}* that are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, does there exist a bijection f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that f and f⁻¹ are computable in deterministic polynomial time and, for every string x, x∈A if and only if f(x)∈B?
definitions: A language is a set of finite binary strings, including a specified membership decision for every string; malformed encodings are therefore part of the language convention. NP consists of languages L for which x∈L exactly when some witness of length polynomial in |x| is accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. A many-one reduction from L to A is a total deterministic polynomial-time function g with x∈L iff g(x)∈A. A is NP-complete if A∈NP and every L∈NP reduces to A in this sense. The desired f is a permutation of all finite binary strings, taking members to members and nonmembers to nonmembers. Its running time is polynomial in its input length, and its inverse has a polynomial bound in the inverse input length. The algorithms and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed pair A,B, but not on the particular input string. No advice, oracle, randomness or length-preservation requirement is allowed. This is the unconditional conjecture; P≠NP is not an assumption.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence of these polynomial-time bijections, or prove that two NP-complete languages admit no such bijection with a polynomial-time inverse. A candidate reduction that is not invertible does not refute the conjecture, because a different bijection may exist. Mutual many-one reductions, mutual injective reductions alone, an isomorphism with advice, or a result for only a restricted class of NP-complete languages does not establish the stated claim.
context:
NP-completeness normally identifies problems by their ability to simulate one another. A reduction may map many distinct instances to the same target instance, leave most target strings unused, and erase information that would be needed to reconstruct its input. The isomorphism conjecture asks for a much more rigid relationship: an efficiently reversible relabelling of the entire instance space. Its claim includes every artificially constructed NP-complete language, not only the familiar examples used in applications.

The distinction is visible in the quantifiers. Choosing one clever reduction from SAT to another problem and discovering that it is many-to-one says nothing decisive about whether some other reduction could be a bijection. Conversely, an abstract bijection between two infinite sets is not enough: it might take exponential time to compute or invert. The conjecture requires both computations to be efficient, while allowing a polynomial change in the lengths of instances.

Padding supplies the strongest classical evidence. A paddable language has an efficient injective way to append arbitrary recoverable auxiliary information without changing the answer. For satisfiability, fresh variables and a suitably delimited formula encoding can carry extra bits while preserving whether the original formula has a satisfying assignment. Berman and Hartmanis used padding to show that the standard NP-complete examples known at the time are polynomial-time isomorphic. The unresolved step is proving that arbitrary complete languages possess enough recoverable structure.

The conjecture implies P≠NP, but its negation does not automatically imply P≠NP. To see the first point, suppose P=NP. Then the nontrivial languages {0} and 0{0,1}* would both be NP-complete: decide the source problem and output a fixed yes string or no string. Yet a bijection preserving membership cannot map a one-element yes-set onto an infinite yes-set. This elementary obstruction also explains why the unconditional conjecture must be distinguished from its version conditional on P≠NP.

A more subtle possible obstruction starts with an injective, length-nondecreasing polynomial-time function h and the image h(SAT). This image is still NP-complete: h is a reduction, and a nondeterministic verifier can guess a short preimage and a satisfying assignment. If h is difficult to invert, the obvious renaming fails. But that difficulty alone does not rule out a different efficient isomorphism. The 2022 Hartmanis problem column discusses how stronger scrambling properties and the possibility of easy cylinders bear on this approach.

Oracle results go in both directions. Kurtz, Mahaney and Royer construct random-oracle counterexamples using scrambling functions. Fenner, Fortnow and Kurtz construct a different oracle setting in which the conjecture holds. These are results about relativized computation, where the algorithms can query a supplied set. They do not settle the ordinary conjecture, but they show that an argument valid uniformly across all such oracle settings cannot choose its truth value.

Restricting the completeness reductions can produce affirmative theorems. Agrawal, Allender and Rudich prove an isomorphism theorem for sets complete under nonuniform AC⁰ reductions, with nonuniform depth-three AC⁰ circuits computing the isomorphisms and their inverses. Here AC⁰ means polynomial-size Boolean circuits of constant depth with unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and negations. Both the restricted completeness hypothesis and the availability of nonuniform circuits matter; dropping them would be a stronger statement.

Agrawal and Watanabe further relate structural assumptions about one-way functions to nonuniform isomorphisms. Under their stated hypotheses they obtain P/poly isomorphisms, permitting polynomial advice that depends on input length. This does not provide the uniform polynomial-time algorithms demanded here. The broad question remains whether NP-completeness itself forces reversible structure, or whether some complete languages have an intrinsically different organization of their yes and no instances.
why: A fundamental test of what NP-completeness means beyond mutual reducibility: does it impose one efficiently reversible structure on all complete decision problems? It links padding, cryptographic inversion, uniformity and the limitations of relativizing methods.

importance.reason: A defining structural-complexity conjecture about the entire NP-complete degree, stronger than P≠NP and supported by substantial restricted-model theorems and oracle barriers.

progress.text: Berman–Hartmanis prove isomorphism for paddable complete languages and formulate the unrestricted conjecture.
Kurtz–Mahaney–Royer present random-oracle counterexamples at STOC; a journal treatment follows in 1995.
Fenner–Fortnow–Kurtz publish an oracle relative to which the conjecture holds.
Agrawal–Allender–Rudich prove the nonuniform AC⁰ isomorphism and gap theorems.
Agrawal–Watanabe give conditional nonuniform structural results involving one-way functions and easy cylinders.
The Hartmanis open-problems column retains the full conjecture and discusses the remaining cylinder and reduction questions.

status_note: The unrestricted uniform conjecture remains explicitly open in the 2022 primary-author problem column. A search for later results through 11 September 2026 found no resolution; restricted nonuniform theorems and oracle results do not establish it.
